title: Transcriptomic signatures and network‐based methods uncover new senescent cell anti‐apoptotic pathways and senolytics

sections.abstract:
Cellular senescence is an irreversible cell cycle arrest caused by various stressors that damage cells. Over time, senescent cells accumulate and contribute to the progression of multiple age‐related degenerative diseases. It is believed that these cells accumulate partly due to their ability to evade programmed cell death through the development and activation of survival and antiapoptotic resistance mechanisms; however, many aspects of how these survival mechanisms develop and activate are still unknown. By analyzing transcriptomic signature profiles generated by the LINCS L1000 project and using network‐based methods, we identified various genes that could represent new senescence‐related survival mechanisms. Additionally, employing the same methodology, we identified over 600 molecules with potential senolytic activity. Experimental validation of our computational findings confirmed the senolytic activity of Fluorouracil, whose activity would be mediated by a multitarget mechanism, revealing that its targets AURKA, EGFR, IRS1, SMAD4, and KRAS are new senescent cell antiapoptotic pathways (SCAPs). The development of these pathways could depend on the stimulus that induces cellular senescence. The SCAP development and activation mechanisms proposed in this work offer new insights into how senescent cells survive. Identifying new antiapoptotic resistance targets and drugs with potential senolytic activity paves the way for developing new pharmacological therapies to eliminate senescent cells selectively.

Keywords: aging, SCAPs, senescence, senolytics, survival networks
sections.introduction:
Cellular senescence (CS) is a state of irreversible cell cycle arrest in response to various stressors that can damage cells. These agents include telomere shortening, oncogenic activation, ionizing radiation, and oxidative stress [ 1 ]. Senescent cells (SCs) exhibit various morphological and molecular alterations, such as acquiring an elongated and flattened phenotype in cell cultures, accumulating lysosomes and misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm, and alterations in mitochondrial dynamics. Additionally, they also secrete various soluble components into the extracellular medium, such as cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and metalloproteins, collectively known as the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which can profoundly modify and influence the cellular microenvironment [ 2 ]. CS is widely recognized as a tumor suppressor mechanism [ 3 ]; Additionally, they play multiple roles in normal physiology, such as wound healing, immunomodulation, regeneration, development, and cellular structure [ 4 ]. However, it has also been demonstrated that the accumulation of SCs is implicated in the onset and progression of multiple chronic‐degenerative diseases associated with aging, including cancer [ 5 ]. Senescent cells cannot respond to pro‐apoptotic stimuli, leading to their accumulation in organs and tissues over time [ 6 ] due to the development and activation of various survival and antiapoptotic resistance pathways (SCAPs) [ 1 ], such as the PI3K/AKT, p53, BCL‐2 family, and heat shock proteins (HSPs) signaling pathways [ 7 ]. The first SCAPs were discovered through bioinformatic analysis of transcriptomic data generated from gene inhibition with small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). In total, 39 genes were found that induced selective death of SCs when individually inhibited. This finding led to the discovery of the first senolytic molecules, Dasatinib and Quercetin, which are small molecules capable of inducing selective death of SCs through various mechanisms [ 8 ].

The Library of Integrated Network‐based Cellular Signatures (LINCS L1000) project is a biomedical initiative focused on generating molecular signatures of human cells in response to various chemical and genetic perturbations. It utilizes a large‐scale gene expression technology to measure changes in the expression of approximately 1000 highly representative genes. These genes have been carefully selected to represent the global human transcriptome. The idea is that analyzing the changes in these genes after exposure to different drugs or genetic modifications makes it possible to infer broader patterns of gene activity [ 9 ].

In this work, our objective was to identify new SCAPs. For this purpose, we analyzed the transcriptomic signatures generated by the LINCS L1000 project, where individual genes are silenced using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs). These transcriptomic profiles provide a rich and detailed database to analyze gene expression changes associated with the inhibition of genes that, when inhibited, generate the same biological response. Thus, we pinpointed genes whose suppression elicits a transcriptomic response akin to that observed when known SCAPs are inhibited. Then, with these genes, we constructed and analyzed gene co‐expression networks (GCNs) using gene expression profiles from human lung samples to determine whether the newly identified genes are functionally related to each other and known SCAPs, which would place the identified genes as probable SCAPs. We then used network pharmacology to identify inhibitors of the proteins encoded by the new SCAP candidates. The computational findings were experimentally validated using two distinct models of senescence in primary cultures of normal human lung fibroblasts, one of replicative senescence (RS) and the other of stress‐induced premature senescence (SIPS). Two of the drugs identified through network‐based methods inhibited the new SCAPs in the two senescence models. Figure 1 graphically summarizes the general strategy used in this work.

General methodology. The analysis begins with transcriptomic signature similarity using LINCS‐L1000 data, leading to the identification of 154 SCAP candidates through clustering based on distance correlation (dCor). Next, co‐expression networks (GCNs) are inferred from GTEx lung expression data using ARACNe, followed by filtering to refine 120 candidate genes. These candidates are integrated into a drug‐gene interaction network using DGIdb, identifying 44 targets and 620 drugs. Finally, experimental validation of selected drugs (PF‐562271 and fluorouracil) in replicative (RS) and stress‐induced senescence (SIPS) models confirms new SCAPs targets and senolytics with therapeutic potential.
sections.methods:
Consensus transcriptomic signatures data were used, condensing the signature profiles generated by the individual shRNA silencing of 4362 genes in nine different cell lines [ 38 ]. Of the original 39 SCAPs, 29 were available within the signature's dataset. Only the 978 landmark genes quantified in the original LINCS L1000 platform were considered for the similarity calculations.

The distance correlation (dCor) was chosen as a similarity measure, which considers the difference between the joint and marginal distributions of two variables. Unlike Pearson's correlation, which only measures linear relationships, dCor can detect nonlinear and more complex interactions. A zero value indicates total independence, while higher values indicate greater dependence [ 39 ]. The dCor was calculated using the distance correlation function implemented in the dCor 0.5 package [ 40 ], and hierarchical clustering analysis was performed using the clustermap function and the average method implemented in the seaborn 0.11.2 package [ 41 ].

The statistical significance of the similarity of the SCAPs signatures was obtained by bootstrapping [ 42 ]. The dCor of each pair of genes within the original set of 4362 signatures was calculated, then random samples of the same size as the reference sample were taken, and the number of times the random samples had a median dCor higher than the reference was calculated through 100 000 simulations.

We randomly selected 22 genes (simulating 21 SCAPs and 1 candidate) and calculated their median dCor values. After one million simulations, we used the highest random dCor value (0.405) as the cutoff. We visualized the genes whose signatures were similar to those of the SCAPs through a network generated using cytoscape 3.10.1 [ 43 ].

The Genotype‐Tissue Expression (GTEx) project provides gene expression data generated through bulk RNA‐seq from 53 different tissues, collected from 714 donors without reported diseases whose ages ranged from 20 to 79 years [ 44 ].

The dataset of raw counts was obtained. In this original dataset, each sample included counts for a total of 56 200 genes for each of the 53 tissues. The dataset was divided into two different datasets: young individuals (20–39 years) and old individuals (60–70 years). Only tissues with more than 25 samples in each age group were selected, resulting in 33 tissues. The tissues and the number of samples per group used for the analyses are shown in Table 1 .

The tissue and the number of samples per group used for the analyses.

The raw gene expression count values for each tissue sample were preprocessed as follows: Initially, the mean of the counts for each gene across the samples was calculated. Genes with a mean below 10 were removed, and genes with zero count values in more than 50% of the samples were discarded [ 45 ]. Subsequently, the dataset was quantile normalized using the qnorm 0.8.1 library. The next step consisted of dividing the dataset into two groups according to the ages defined by the GTEx project: young (20–39 years old) and old (60–70 years old). Protein‐coding genes, long noncoding RNAs, microRNAs, pseudogenes, and other types of RNA species were retained.

GCNs were inferred using mutual information (MI) to measure gene co‐expression. Mutual information is a statistical measure that quantifies how much information one random variable, such as gene expression, contains about another. The ARACNe (Algorithm for the Reconstruction of Gene Regulatory Networks) algorithm, one of the most popular methods for inferring GCNs, calculates the MI between two data series [ 46 ]. ARACNe was applied to both preprocessed datasets (young and old) to establish correlations between gene pairs. The complete transcriptome networks were calculated for all datasets. To speed up the calculation, we used the multicore C++ version without adaptive partitioning inference [ 47 ]. This version is available at https://github.com/josemaz/aracne‐multicore .

To obtain statistically significant networks, we followed this methodology: For each of the 33 tissues in both young and elderly individuals, we calculated the GCN of the complete transcriptome. We then removed all interactions below the 95th percentile of MI values for each GCN, retaining only the top 5% of the total interactions. From this subset, we extracted the interactions for both the SCAPs and the 154 candidate genes.

Using the MI values of the complete transcriptome, the MI value corresponding to the 95th percentile of each network (young and elderly) in each tissue was obtained. These values were then used as a cutoff in each constructed GCN to obtain statistically significant networks. To investigate the interactions conserved across different tissues, an analysis was performed using the Jaccard index to measure the similarity between the sets of gene interactions in each tissue. The Jaccard index is calculated as the size of the intersection of two sets divided by the size of their union, which quantifies the similarity between the network interactions. The result was then visualized using the heatmap function from the Seaborn 0.13 library.

To check the consistency between the transcriptomic signature network in Fig. 1B and the GCNs of elderly tissues in Fig. 4C , we measured their similarity, that is, the same genes connected by the same edges. First, we obtained the largest cluster from each GCN, and from this cluster, we subtracted the interactions between SCAPs, leaving only the interactions between the candidates and the SCAPs. Then, we quantified how many interactions from the transcriptomic signature network were present in each of the GCNs. To determine the statistical significance of the number of conserved interactions between the transcriptomic signature network and each GCN, we used a hypergeometric test. Briefly, for each network, we considered each pair of interactions as a unique element, and we used the following data: N = 16 104 (the total number of pairs of interactions of the 154 candidates), n (the total number of elements in each aged tissue GCNs), m = 1800 (the total number of elements in the transcriptomic signature network), and k (the intersection between n and m ). To calculate the probability, we used the formula of the hypergeometric distribution:

The genes that comprise the human lung co‐expression network of the 120 candidates and known SCAPs (elderly network) were enriched within Gene Ontology categories 2023 and KEGG Pathways 2021 to observe the biological processes and signaling pathways to which they belong. For this purpose, we used Enrichr https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/ through its GSEApy API [ 48 ]. The Adjusted P ‐value < 0.05 option was used to determine statistical significance, and the 4362 genes from the LINCS dataset were used as background. Redundant terms were manually eliminated to show only the 10 most enriched terms.

To construct the network of senolytic drugs and their targets, 59 senolytic drugs and 550 targets reported in previous work were used [ 49 ]. We applied bootstrapping to determine whether the genes from the GCN were enriched in senolytic drug targets. Specifically, the 4362 genes from the LINCS L1000 dataset were used as background, and one million simulations were performed. In each simulation, 120 elements were randomly selected (the same number as the genes in the GCN without considering the original SCAP genes), and the frequency with which these random elements matched elements within the network of 550 senolytic drug targets was calculated.

The Drug Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb) v4.2.0 [ 50 ] was used for drug repositioning. This database compiles information from 22 other pharmacological databases (consulted on 03/05/2024). The search for molecules for the 120 GCN genes resulted in 620 drugs interacting uniquely with 44 of the 120 GCN genes.

Human lung fibroblasts from the CCD‐8Lu primary cell line (RRID: CVCL_2398), acquired from ATCC (catalog number: CCL‐201). The cell line used was authenticated by ATCC (Manassas, VA, USA). The cells were cultured in 100‐mm Petri dishes and maintained in Gibco™ (Grand Island, NY, USA) DMEM/F‐12 culture medium (catalog number: 11320033), supplemented with 10% heat‐inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS) from Gibco™ (catalog number: 16000044) and 1% penicillin, amphotericin B, and streptomycin, also from Gibco™ (catalog number: 15240‐062). The cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . All experiments were performed with Mycoplasma‐free cells.

Approximately 10 000 cells with PD < 10 were seeded in 48‐well plates and incubated for 2 h. After this time, most cells adhered to the culture plate and were subsequently exposed to H 2 O 2 (Sigma‐Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA), cat. H1009) at 100, 150, and 200 μ m concentrations. After 2 h, two washes with 1× PBS were performed, and fresh medium was added. At 24 h, the medium was renewed. The cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . On subsequent days (3, 6, and 9) after H 2 O 2 treatment, the cells were detached using 0.05% trypsin. Cell viability was evaluated in three independent experiments using the trypan blue technique, each in triplicate.

Statistical analysis was performed with prism 8.0.2. (GraphPad Inc., Boston, MA, USA) The Shapiro–Wilk test was applied for normality analysis, with a significance level of P < 0.05. A two‐way ANOVA was used to analyze the peroxide concentration that reduces proliferation over 9 days, followed by a Tukey's post hoc test, using a significance level of P < 0.05.

To establish a RS model, cells at a low passage number (< 10) were seeded into six‐well plates, and the culture medium was refreshed every 48 h. Once the cells attained approximately 80% confluency, they were detached using 500 μL of 0.05% trypsin per well. Subsequently, the cells were reseeded at a 1 : 4 ratio across new six‐well plates, a subculturing process where cells from the original culture were divided into four separate plates. This subculturing process was repeated until the cells achieved a high passage number (> 60). Upon reaching passage 60, 10 000 high‐passage cells were seeded in new plates and allowed to stabilize for 24 h to accommodate their reduced adherence capacity. After this stabilization period, 10 000 low‐passage cells (< 10) were also seeded in 48‐well plates to monitor and quantify their proliferation on Days 3, 6, and 9.

Cell viability was determined by the trypan blue exclusion staining assay. Senescent cells were seeded according to the protocols described above. Senescent and proliferating cells were detached by treatment with 0.05% trypsin for 5 min; trypsin was neutralized with an equal proportion of medium with 10% FBS. We mixed 10 μL of cell suspension to count cells with 10 μL of trypan blue. Then, we used 10 μL of this mixture in the Bio‐Rad (Hercules, CA, USA) TC20™ automated counter (catalog: 145‐0101).

The SA‐β‐gal assay was prepared following the protocol previously reported in the literature [ 51 ]. The assay was carried out for cells treated with 200 μ m H 2 O 2 at 72 h, defining established senescence as a percentage greater than 60% of positive cells. In the case of high passage cells (> 65), the assay was performed 24 h after seeding, taking established senescence as a percentage greater than 60% of senescent cells.

Senescence induction was carried out according to the described protocols, using poly‐ l ‐lysine‐free glass coverslips in six‐well plates. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 15 min at room temperature. Afterward, they were washed twice with PBS and incubated with 0.1% Triton X‐100 for 45 min to permeabilize the cells. Subsequently, the cells were washed three times with PBS. Next, they were incubated with 0.1% Tween and 3% albumin for 90 min to block nonspecific sites, followed by three washes with PBS. All antibodies (AB) were used to measure the senescent state at a 1 : 250 dilution. The selected markers were Lamin B1 (HAB8982, Abcam (Cambridge, UK)), p21 (#6246, Santa Cruz (Dallas, TX, USA)), and GLB1 (ab220283, Abcam).

The antiactive caspase‐3 antibody (ab32042, Abcam) was used to evaluate the apoptosis caused by the drugs at a 1 : 100 concentration. The ABs were diluted in 0.1% PBS‐Tween, and each sample was incubated with 50 μL of AB for 24 h at 4 °C with gentle agitation, followed by three washes with PBS; the secondary ABs were used at a 1 : 1000 dilution; the following ABs were used: Goat anti‐Mouse IgG (H + L) Cross‐Adsorbed Secondary Antibody, Alexa Fluor™ 594 (A11005, Invitrogen (Carlsbad, CA, USA)), Goat anti‐Mouse IgG (H + L) Cross‐Adsorbed Secondary Antibody, Alexa Fluor™ 488 (A11001), and Alexa Fluor® 594 AffiniPure™ Goat Anti‐Mouse IgG (H + L) (115‐585‐003, Jackson Immunoresearch (West Grove, PA, USA)) and Goat anti‐Rabbit IgG (H + L) Cross‐Adsorbed Secondary Antibody, Alexa Fluor™ 488 (A11008, Invitrogen). The secondary ABs were diluted in 0.1% PBS‐Tween, and each sample was incubated with 50 μL for 1 h at room temperature in complete darkness and without agitation, followed by three washes with PBS. The coverslips with the cells were mounted on 50 μL of the mounting solution on glass slides. The mounting solution was prepared using 500 μL of distilled water and 500 μL of glycerol, to which 1 μL of 4′,6‐diamidino‐2‐phenylindole (DAPI) (D1306, Invitrogen) was added. The coverslips with the cells were mounted on 50 μL of the mounting solution on glass slides.

Images were obtained using the Zeiss AXIOVERT 40 CFL microscope and processed with the zen 2.3 (Blue edition, Zeiss Group, Oberkochen, Germany) software. A Python script was performed for fluorescence quantification and statistical analysis.

For the biological assays, the following compounds were used: Fluorouracil (PHR1227, Sigma Aldrich), PF‐562271 (PZ0387, Sigma Aldrich), Dasatinib (CDS023389, Sigma Aldrich), and Quercetin (PHR1488, Sigma Aldrich). All compounds to be evaluated were dissolved in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (D5879, Sigma Aldrich) to obtain a 100 m m stock solution. Subsequently, dilutions of each drug were prepared in 10% FBS culture medium without antibiotics, reaching a final concentration of 100 μ m with 0.1% DMSO. For the positive control, a combination of Dasatinib and Quercetin (D + Q) with concentrations of 250 n m for D and 50 μ m for Q was used [ 15 ]. Additionally, medium with FBS without antibiotics and 0.1% DMSO was prepared. All solutions were filtered with a 0.22 μm pore size filter. The different concentrations used to evaluate senolytic activity were obtained by serial dilutions from the 100 μ m solution.

Approximately 15 000 cells were seeded in 96‐well plates for both SIPS (day 6) and RS and approximately 10 000 proliferating cells (passage < 10) were seeded. The RS and proliferating cells were incubated for 24 h at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 before treatment application. After this period, the proliferating cells reached approximately a population of 15 000 cells. 200 μL of each drug for each concentration studied, and the vehicle group (0.1% DMSO) and the positive control (D + Q) were added. Based on a standard protocol for evaluating senolytic compounds, the cells were incubated for 48 h under the same temperature and CO 2 conditions [ 52 ]. After this time, a double wash with PBS was performed. A 3‐(4,5‐dimethylthiazol‐2‐yl)‐2,5‐diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) (M2128, Invitrogen) solution was prepared at a final concentration of 0.5 mg·mL −1 and pH 7.4, which was passed through a 0.22 μm filter. 100 μL of the MTT solution was added to each well, and the cells were incubated for 2 h at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 in complete darkness. After incubation, the MTT was removed, and 150 μL of DMSO was added. The plates were gently shaken for 10 min and then incubated for another 15 min at 37 °C. The relative optical density was quantified using a Multiskan SkyHigh microplate spectrophotometer (catalog number: A51119500C, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Before reading the absorbance at 570 nm, the plates were shaken for 10 s. Each drug at each concentration was evaluated in three independent experiments in triplicate.

The spectrophotometer readings were processed as follows: the Shapiro–Wilk normality test was applied, considering a P ‐value < 0.05 as significant. Then, a one‐way ANOVA test was performed, accepting a P ‐value < 0.05 as significant. This was followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test with a Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment to reduce the false discovery rate (FDR), also considering a P ‐value < 0.05 as significant. All analyses were performed using prism 8.0.2.
sections.results:
We based our approach on the hypothesis that silencing genes that promote the selective death of SCs generates a similar transcriptomic response to identify new SCAPs. We employed transcriptomic signature data from the LINCS L1000 project to verify our hypothesis. We used the consensus signature profiles, which, through robust z‐scores, condensed the signature profiles of nine cell lines into a single profile.

The first step was determining similarities between the signatures caused by inhibiting known SCAP genes. As previously mentioned, we employed the distance correlation (dCor) to measure this similarity, which can detect both linear and nonlinear associations. In Fig. 2A , we present a hierarchical clustering analysis based on the median dCor, which revealed the existence of two clusters: The first consists of 15 genes (BCL2, GK3B, ABL1, CHEK1, PIK3CB, FYN, HIF1A, KIT, EFNB3, PIK3CG, AKT1, PTK2, ABL2, KDR, and SRC) with a median dCor = 0.390, P = 3 × 10 −5 , and the second group includes six genes (PIK3CA, PPM1L, FLT1, SERPINB2, BCL2L11, and MCL1) with a median dCor = 0.469, P = 0.00073. Considering both clusters, the 21 genes have a median dCor = 0.305, which is higher than expected by chance, P = 0.00054. The clustering based on the signature profiles of the SCAP genes suggests the existence of multiple independent survival and antiapoptotic resistance mechanisms; however, some genes showed high similarities in their signature patterns. Therefore, we decided to group the two identified clusters into a single group of 21 genes.

Similarity of the transcriptomic signatures of SCAPs. (A) Hierarchical clustering analysis based on correlation distance. A group of 15 similar SCAP genes was identified, showing a median distance correlation (dCor), dCor = 0.390, P = 3 × 10 −5 , and another group of six SCAP genes with a median dCor = 0.469, P = 0.00073. The 21 SCAP genes present a median dCor = 0.305, P = 0.00054. (B) The inhibition of 154 individual genes (gray nodes) causes a transcriptomic signature similar (dCor > 0.405) to that observed when inhibiting the 21 SCAPs represented by yellow nodes, where the size of these nodes indicates the number of individual genes showing a similar signature profile.

We grouped the two clusters, one with 15 genes and one with six genes, into a single group of 21 highly correlated genes, as both clusters might represent unique survival mechanisms that, although independent, share certain similarities. For subsequent analyses, we chose to use only the 21 genes in the cluster instead of the 29 SCAPs from the full dataset, as the inclusion of the remaining eight genes, which do not cluster in any cluster, might introduce unnecessary noise and variability into the analysis. Having signature profiles generated by the inhibition of 4362 individual genes, we can identify those genes that, when inhibited, cause a signature similar to that observed in the group of 21 original SCAP genes, which could trigger the same cellular response, selective death of SCs. We then calculated the median similarity in the signature of each of the 4462 genes concerning the group of 21 SCAPs. Figure 2B shows the 154 genes (the complete list is in the Figure S1 ) that, when inhibited, generate a transcriptomic response such as the inhibition of the 21 original SCAP genes together, showing a dCor > 0.405 (cutoff established in Materials and methods). The similarity between these genes is visualized through a network, where the size of the yellow nodes (SCAPs) reflects the number of genes (gray nodes) that induce a signature similar to that of the SCAP genes.

The individual inhibition of the 39 SCAP genes triggers the selective death of SCs and causes a similar transcriptomic signature. These findings suggest a functional relationship among the SCAP genes. For this reason, we decided to explore the correlation between these genes. For this purpose, we constructed GCNs using gene expression data from the human lung and 32 other tissues of young (20–39 years) and old (60–70 years) individuals obtained from the GTEx project. We used MI as a metric to quantify the statistical dependence between gene pairs, as shown in Fig. 3 .

Gene co‐expression network (GCN) analysis of SCAPs. (A) GCN of SCAP genes in human lung from young (20–39 years) and elderly (60–70 years) individuals. (B) Loss and gain of edges in GCNs with age. (C) Using the Jaccard index, the similarity (same genes connected by the same edges) of GCNs from 33 tissues in young and elderly individuals was quantified.

As shown in panel (A), SCAP genes are co‐expressed in human lung tissue in both young and old individuals. However, the network in the elderly loses connections.

This phenomenon of SCAP GCN disconnection during aging is expected but not uniform across other aging tissues, as shown in panel (B). In tissues such as the vagina, testis, skin, pancreas, ovary, minor salivary gland, heart, colon, and adrenal gland, the SCAP gene networks gain connections with age. Moreover, the networks neither lose nor gain connections in tissues such as blood and sun‐exposed skin.

However, the loss or gain of connections in SCAP GCNs is not the only phenomenon occurring. As shown in panel C, SCAP GCNs undergo rewiring with age. To measure this, we used the Jaccard index to measure network similarity (the same genes are connected by the same edges). In addition to revealing the change in co‐expression patterns of SCAPs in aging tissues, it shows that SCAP GCNs from different tissues have low similarity. This result suggests that the functional organization of SCAPs depends on the tissue and not just on age.

Based on the hypothesis that SCAP genes are co‐expressed and that the wiring of their networks changes with age and is tissue‐dependent, we investigated whether the 154 genes that induce a transcriptomic signature similar to that of the SCAP genes are co‐expressed with each other and with the SCAP genes in the lung and other tissues of both, young and elderly individuals, as shown in Fig. 4 .

Gene co‐expression network (GCN) analysis of SCAP candidates. (A) GCN of SCAPs and candidate genes in human lungs from young and elderly individuals. (B) Loss and gain of edges in GCNs with age. (C) Using the Jaccard index, the similarity (same genes connected by the same edges) of GCNs from 33 tissues in young and elderly individuals was quantified.

As shown in panel (A), both SCAP genes and candidates are co‐expressed in young and elderly individuals. However, similar to the GCNs of SCAP genes alone, the networks (considering only the candidate genes connections and not the SCAP connections) in the elderly exhibits fewer edges (571 edges in the elderly vs. 765 in young individuals) and slightly fewer genes (120 candidate genes in the elderly vs. 147 candidate genes in young individuals). This observation suggests that aging affects not only the connectivity but also the number of genes involved in these GCNs. The phenomenon of network disconnection in the elderly remains common but not uniform across tissues, as illustrated in panel (B). Interestingly, practically the same tissues continue to gain and loss connections during aging, as previously observed in the analysis of SCAP genes alone.

This consistency reinforces the notion that age‐related changes in gene co‐expression patterns are tissue‐specific and not only limited to SCAP genes but also extend to our candidate genes. As shown in panel (C), the networks of candidate genes exhibit a behavior similar to those of SCAP genes. Specifically, the networks of young and elderly individuals maintain a relative similarity, while networks from different tissues do not.

Additionally, we analyzed the consistency between the transcriptomic signature network in Fig. 2B and the aged lung tissue network in Fig. 4A . Interestingly, we found that both networks share 47 connections ( P = 3 × 10 −5 , hypergeometric test), meaning that the same links connect the same genes. This result reinforces that the inhibited genes in the network in Fig. 2B , which cause a similar perturbation as SCAPs, are also functionally related to SCAPs. Interestingly, in the other aged tissue networks, shared links with the transcriptomic perturbation network are also found (Figure S1 ). These results suggest that genes that cause a similar perturbation to SCAPs when inhibited might indeed be novel SCAPs, as they are also co‐expressed in multiple tissues.

Assuming that there is a higher number of SCs during aging and that apoptosis evasion results from rewiring SCAPs GCNs, we selected the elderly GCN from Fig. 4A as our system for study and experimentation to better understand SC survival mechanisms; therefore, we considered only the 120 candidate genes that are connected within the network for the following analyses. This densely connected GCN could represent a well‐defined transcriptional survival program. We performed a functional enrichment analysis of the complete network to investigate this hypothesis, as shown in Fig. 5 .

Enrichment analysis of significant genes across biological processes and KEGG pathways. (A) Enrichment of significant genes in biological processes identified through Gene Ontology (GO) analysis. The x ‐axis represents the −log10 of the False Discovery Rate (FDR), and the size of each dot corresponds to the number of genes associated with each process. Colors reflect the magnitude of the −log10(FDR), with darker shades indicating stronger significance. (B) Enrichment of significant genes in KEGG pathways. Similar to panel (A), the x ‐axis shows the −log10(FDR), while the size and color of the dots indicate the number of genes and the level of statistical significance, respectively. Top enriched pathways include the PI3K‐Akt signaling pathway, focal adhesion, and ErbB signaling pathway, highlighting the 120 SCAP candidates are part of multiple mechanisms of survival and evasion of programmed cell death.

Panel (A) shows the 10 most enriched biological processes, where we primarily find processes associated with protein modification (phosphorylation and autophosphorylation) as well as processes related to signal transduction, cell migration, and proliferation. Interestingly, processes related to cell death also emerge, such as negative regulation of extrinsic apoptosis and anoikis, a specific form of apoptosis that occurs mainly in epithelial and endothelial tissues. Additionally, signaling pathways (KEGG pathways) were analyzed as shown in panel (B), where it is observed that pathways such as PI3K‐Akt, ErbB, JAK–STAT, and HIF‐1, classically related to survival and apoptosis evasion, are enriched. These results suggest that the 120 candidates that make up the network along with the SCAPs are part of multiple mechanisms of survival and evasion of programmed cell death.

Identifying 120 potential SCAP genes represents a significant advance for discovering and repositioning senolytic molecules. As shown in Fig. 6 , we adopted a network pharmacology approach to explore this possibility.

Drug‐target networks. (A) A total of 620 molecules (red nodes) interacts with 44 of the 120 candidate genes (green nodes). Several of these molecules interact with more than one target, as observed through the nodes' color and size gradient. (B) Druggable target network, showing the 10 drugs with the highest number of targets within the GCN. The colors of pie‐charted nodes represent the drugs that influence those proteins.

To explore whether our 120 candidates can function as pharmacological targets and direct small molecules to eliminate SC selectively, we analyzed whether they are targets of known senolytics. As shown in Fig. S1 , we constructed a drug–target network that includes 550 targets of 59 senolytic drugs reported in the literature. Notably, 18 of our candidates (green nodes: KRAS, EGFR, JAK1, BLM, HRAS, TUBB2A, HMGB1, WRN, SMAD4, ERBB3, AKT3, VIM, CRKL, DYRK3, RUVBL2, DROSHA, IL15, and PPIA) are effective targets of senolytics, with an overlap greater than expected by chance ( P = 0.0043, bootstrapping). This result validates that our methodology has succeeded in identifying targets that, when pharmacologically inhibited, induce selective death of SCs. Therefore, these 18 candidates are proposed as new SCAP genes.

The fact that multiple genes from the 120 identified as potential SCAPs are targets of known senolytics allowed us to identify and propose molecules that, by inhibiting these targets, could act as potential senolytics. Using the DGIdb database, we identified molecules that interact with the candidate genes, as shown in Fig. 6A . We found 620 molecules (red nodes) interacting with 44 of the 120 candidate genes. Notably, several of these molecules interact with more than one candidate gene, observed in the network through a color gradient and a progressive increase in node size, reflecting the number of targets with which each molecule interacts. The complete list of the 620 potential senolytics and their respective targets is available in Table S1 .

Using the GCN of elderly lung from Fig. 4A and focusing only on the genes not belonging to the original SCAPs, and the 10 drugs with the highest number of targets identified in network 6B, we constructed a druggable target network, as shown in Fig. 4C . We found that these 10 multitarget drugs interact with 14 genes from the GCN. Our results suggest that the pharmacological inhibition of these 14 targets could induce selective death of senescent cells, implying a potential senolytic effect for the drugs identified in network 4B. To validate the antiapoptotic activity of the proposed targets, and the molecules with potential senolytic activity, we selected the molecules Fluorouracil and PF‐562271 based on criteria of cost, commercial availability, and the number of targets they inhibit.

To validate our computational findings, we developed two senescence models using primary cultures of human lung fibroblasts from the CCD8‐Lu cell line, as shown in Fig. 7 . For the SIPS model, oxidative stress was induced with H 2 O 2 . As observed in panel (A), different concentrations (100, 150, and 200 μ m ) of H 2 O 2 were evaluated. The 200 μ m concentration was selected for senescence induction since, as shown in panels (B) and (C), the cells exhibited characteristic senescence features and markers at this concentration. For the RS model, cells at a high passage (> 60) were used, showing a reduction in proliferation, as shown in panel (D). Additionally, as shown in panels (E) and (F), at this passage, the cells exhibited classic senescence features and markers.

Standardization of two senescence models using the CCD8‐Lu cell line. (A) Stress‐induced premature senescence (SIPS). Cell proliferation curves with 100, 150, and 200 μ m H 2 O 2 treatments. A progressive reduction in proliferation was observed with increasing concentrations. (B) SA‐β‐gal assay of cells treated with 200 μ m H 2 O 2 , around 80% of cells are positive, indicating a high incidence of senescence. (C) Immunofluorescence of Lamin B1 and GLB1 markers in cells treated with 200 μ m H 2 O 2 . (D) Replicative Senescence (RS). Proliferation curves of cells at low passage (< 20) and high passage (> 60). (E) SA‐β‐gal assay of cells treated with 200 μ m H 2 O 2 , around 60% of cells are positive, confirming the effectiveness of the treatment in inducing senescence. (F) Immunofluorescence of Lamin B1, GLB1, and p21 markers in cells treated with 200 μ m H 2 O 2 , reaffirming the presence of senescent markers. The data are presented with the standard error of the mean (SEM) for n = 3 independent experiments performed in triplicate. Mann–Whitney U test. Statistical significance levels are indicated as *P < 0.01, ** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001.

In the MTT assay, we evaluated the functionality of proliferating and senescent cells after being treated with three different concentrations of Fluorouracil (10, 12.5, and 15 μ m ) and PF‐562271 (1, 2.5, and 5 μ m ) for 48 h. Furthermore, the D + Q combination was used as a control to compare senolytic effects, as shown in Fig. 8 . In panel (A), the results indicate that neither Fluorouracil nor PF‐562271 exhibit a significant senolytic effect in the SIPS model; D + Q shows a slight effect, although it is not statistically significant ( P = 0.067). However, as observed in panel (B), treatment with 10 μ m Fluorouracil for 48 h significantly reduced the functionality of SCs ( P < 0.0001) without impacting proliferating cells ( P < 0.0001) in the RS model. The fact that Fluorouracil has a senolytic effect in RS but not SIPS suggests that the activation and development of SCAPs depend on the senescence‐inducing stimulus. Interestingly, the senolytic effect was not intensified by increasing the concentration of Fluorouracil, although it decreased proliferating cells' functionality.

Effect of Fluorouracil and PF‐562271 at three different concentrations for 48 h on the two senescence models. (A) No effect of the two drugs was observed in the Stress‐induced premature senescence (SIPS) model. (B) In the Replicative Senescence (RS) model, Fluorouracil at a concentration of 10 μ m significantly reduced cell functionality after 48 h. (C) Treatment with 10 μ m Fluorouracil for 48 h induced apoptosis in cells under RS but did not affect proliferating cells. The data are presented with the standard error of the mean (SEM) for n = 3 independent experiments performed in triplicate. Mann–Whitney U test. Statistical significance levels are indicated as ns, P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001.

On the other hand, PF‐562271 affected cells in the RS model, unlike the SIPS model; however, this effect was not selective, as it decreased the functionality of both proliferating and senescent cells. This result rules out its potential as a senolytic agent. In both models, it was observed that D + Q did not produce a senolytic effect.

As shown in panel (C), we investigated whether the reduction in the functionality of SCs in the RS model after being treated with 10 μ m Fluorouracil for 48 h could be due to the selective induction of apoptosis. For this, we measured the expression of the active executioner Caspase‐3, crucial in the apoptotic process, by immunofluorescence. The results showed that, in response to Fluorouracil treatment, the intensity of the active Caspase‐3 signal in SCs increased 2.3‐fold compared with nonsenescent cells ( P = 0.0093). This finding suggests that treatment with 10 μ m Fluorouracil for 48 h has a senolytic effect by inducing selective death of SCs; this points to the targets of this drug, including AURKA, EGFR, IRS1, SMAD4, KRAS, as potential new SCAPs.
sections.discussion:
Cellular senescence is a fundamental biological process that serves as a potent barrier against the proliferation of damaged cells, contributing significantly to aging and the suppression of tumorigenesis. Within this context, apoptosis resistance in SCs has garnered significant attention. This resistance is suggested to arise not from inherent cellular traits but rather from the aberrant behavior of certain genes known as SCAPs. This concept is supported by studies, which suggest that SCAPs play a crucial role in modulating cell survival mechanisms that enable senescent cells to evade programmed cell death [ 10 , 11 ].

Further investigations indicate that the upregulation of specific survival and antiapoptotic resistance genes and proteins can elucidate the mechanisms through which senescent cells successfully circumvent apoptosis [ 7 , 12 , 13 ]. This resistance to apoptosis is a key factor in understanding both the beneficial and detrimental roles of senescent cells in organisms. On the one hand, it prevents damaged cells from turning malignant, while on the other, it can contribute to age‐related pathologies by allowing senescent cells to accumulate. Our results add to this understanding by suggesting that the development and activation of SCAPs are highly dynamic and involve complex networks of genes and proteins. These interactions, as evidenced in our analyses in Figs 2 , 3 , 4 , suggest that multiple genes and proteins work together to confer survival advantages to SCs. To further decipher how these genes promote apoptosis resistance, examining the specific molecular and cellular interactions that allow SCAPs to bypass programmed cell death effectively is crucial.

Studying SCAPs is therefore essential for elucidating the fundamental aspects of cellular senescence and identifying potential therapeutic targets that can modulate senescence in age‐related diseases and cancer. By understanding the intricate networks and pathways that underpin SCAPs function, researchers can develop strategies to enhance or inhibit these pathways, potentially leading to interventions that can mitigate the adverse effects of senescent cell accumulation or exploit the tumor‐suppressive properties of cellular senescence.

To study the co‐expression, development, and activation of SCAPs, we selected human lung tissue as our study system because senescence and the discovery of senolytics have been extensively studied in this tissue using human lung fibroblasts from the IMR90 [ 14 ] and WI‐38 [ 15 ] cell lines as experimental models. However, these cell lines are derived from newborns, whereas we used the CCD‐8Lu cell line, which consists of fibroblasts from adult human lungs. In combination with senescence‐inducing stimuli, these cells may better reflect the behavior of SCAPs, as shown in Figs 3 and 4 , where the most significant differences in GCNs are observed in the cultured cells.

Based on the results of the GCN analysis in Figs 3 and 4 , we propose that the antiapoptotic resistance of SCs is an emergent property derived from changes in co‐expression patterns. These changes can alter existing patterns of functional association during the establishment and progression of senescence and may even lead to new patterns of functional association formation. In this way, we propose that the antiapoptotic resistance of SCs is not an aberration but rather a well‐defined, complexly regulated, and highly dynamic cellular program that could vary depending on the cell type, the senescence‐inducing stimulus, and the stage of senescence, as has been reported with SASP [ 16 , 17 ]. Moreover, considering the impact of the microenvironment on cellular senescence, a deeper analysis of how environmental factors contribute to the senescence and survival of senescent cells, particularly in age‐related diseases and cancers, would enhance our understanding of therapeutic targets. Exploring how SCAP genes interact with other cellular pathways critical for metabolism, differentiation, and inflammation could provide insights into their broader biological roles.

Considering the abovementioned concepts, we used various computational tools to discover new SCAPs. These approaches allowed us to identify 154 genes that, when individually inhibited with shRNA, trigger a transcriptomic response similar to that induced by silencing the original SCAP genes. Of these genes, 120 are co‐expressed with each other and with the SCAPs, which is relevant since genes that share co‐expression patterns tend to be functionally related or regulated by the same transcriptional program [ 18 ].

Of these 120 genes, we found that 18 are targets of known senolytics, which leads us to propose them as potential SCAPs. The discovery of these new SCAPs paves the way for the design and synthesis of new molecules and the identification of molecules in the experimental phase or drugs approved by regulatory agencies to reposition them as new senolytics. We have implemented a network pharmacology approach, which has revealed the existence of more than 600 novel molecules with potential senolytic activity. Many of these molecules can potentially act through a multitarget mechanism, a pharmacological paradigm that is particularly promising for combating complex diseases and phenotypes [ 19 ]. This discovery prompts a closer examination of how these molecules could be integrated into existing or new treatment regimens for diseases associated with aging and cancer, enhancing their clinical and therapeutic relevance.

To demonstrate our computational findings' validity and potential application, we conducted a proof‐of‐concept in two distinct senescence models, SIPS and RS, using two drugs identified in our network pharmacology approach, Fluorouracil and PF‐562271. These experiments allowed us to explore and support at least three of our hypotheses: (1) The drugs from our network are potential senolytics. Treatment with 10 μ m Fluorouracil for 48 h reduced the functionality of cells in RS but did not affect proliferating cells; this reduction could be a consequence of the selective induction of apoptosis, as shown in Fig. 8C . Our candidates are new SCAPs: The senolytic effect of Fluorouracil is mediated through multitarget inhibition of AURKA, EGFR, IRS1, SMAD4, and KRAS. However, we hypothesize that this senolytic activity is due to the synergistic effect of multitarget inhibition, as the individual inhibition of any of these new SCAPs would probably not cause selective death of senescent cells. This would be because this new five reported SCAPs collectively form part of a survival network and are not survival genes on their own, at least in the context of senescence. Interestingly, three of these proteins are effective targets of senolytics; AURKA is inhibited by the senolytic R‐406 [ 20 ], EGFR is inhibited by the senolytics Geldanamycin [ 21 ], MK‐2206 [ 22 ], Ganetespib [ 23 ], and Curcumin [ 24 ]. KRAS is inhibited by Panobinostat [ 25 ], MK‐2206 [ 26 ], Navitoclax [ 27 ], and Metformin [ 28 ]. Although SMAD4 is not a target of any known senolytic, it has been shown to inhibit apoptosis [ 29 ], as has IRS1, which, when inhibited, induces selective apoptosis in cancer cells [ 30 ]. Finally, (3) The development of SCAPs depends on the senescence‐inducing stimulus—Fig. 8A,B show that the tested molecules had differential effects. Despite the same experimental conditions, Fluorouracil exhibited a senolytic impact on the RS but not the SIPS model. A similar effect was observed with D + Q, which slightly impacted the SIPS model, although it was not statistically significant, suggesting that SCAPs are activated differentially depending on the senescence‐inducing stimulus.

Our computational prediction identified fluorouracil as a senolytic, but its senolytic effect is observed only at a concentration of 10 μ m . Higher concentrations do not enhance this effect and instead kill normal cells. We propose that this selective action is due to the high heterogeneity within senescent cells. Despite being induced into senescence by the same stimulus and exhibiting classical markers of senescence, the development of SCAPs might vary depending on the stage of senescence. Consequently, some senescent cells may not be eliminated by fluorouracil due to the absence of specific SCAPs.

In contrast, the results for PF‐562271 are particularly intriguing. This drug appears to selectively kill control cells but not senescent ones. PF‐562271 plays a crucial role in cell adhesion and survival signaling in proliferating cells and is also a known inhibitor of focal adhesion kinase (FAK). Control cells, being actively proliferating, depend heavily on FAK signaling for adhesion, migration, and growth. FAK inhibition disrupts these essential processes, leading to apoptosis. However, senescent cells may not rely on these mechanisms, enabling them to evade death caused by PF‐562271. This suggests that senescent cells have restructured their survival pathways, relying on mechanisms independent of FAK to resist apoptosis.

Furthermore, the lack of senolytic activity of PF‐562271 in the SIPS model could be related to differences in survival mechanisms between stress‐induced and replication‐induced senescence. This supports our hypothesis that SCAPs develop differently depending on the senescence‐inducing stimulus. In the RS model, PF‐562271 induces death in both control and senescent cells, indicating that replication‐induced senescent cells may retain some dependence on FAK or related pathways, while the SIPS model may have activated entirely different survival mechanisms. Our computational method has yet to identify these alternative pathways.

Finally, regarding the validation and reliability of our computational predictions, we emphasize that our method is effective. It was designed to identify molecules with potential senolytic activity using a target‐based approach rather than a molecule‐based approach. That is, we did not train our model with data from molecules known to have senolytic activity. Yet, in the network shown in Fig. 6A , several senolytic agents reported in the literature were identified, such as ABT‐737, curcumin, ellagic acid, epigallocatechin gallate, ganetespib, geldanamycin, hesperadin, luteolin, metformin, navitoclax, R‐406, resveratrol, rosmarinic acid, sirolimus, venetoclax, and vincristine, which target many of the genes we identified as new SCAPs. This demonstrates the validity of our method in identifying molecules with senolytic activity. Furthermore, in the same network (Fig. 6A ), sotrastaurin and tanshinone, which we previously reported as novel senolytics in another study [ 31 ], further validate the effectiveness of our method.

In this study, we decided to use D + Q as a positive control at the concentration commonly reported in the literature (250 n m + 50 μ m ). Surprisingly, however, it had no significant effect on either the SIPS or RS models. We hypothesize that several factors could explain this lack of effect, particularly the choice of cell line. The combination of D + Q has demonstrated senolytic effects in other studies using cell lines such as IMR90 [ 8 ] and WI38 [ 15 ], which are derived from the lung tissue of newborns and neonates. In contrast, the CCD‐8Lu cell line that we used originates from the lung tissue of a 48‐year‐old man. Age and sex differences between cell lines could influence the development of SCAPs, which may vary depending on the biological characteristics of the tissues and cells [ 6 , 32 , 33 ]. Studies have shown that the effectiveness of D + Q can vary depending on the disease model and the senescence‐inducing stimulus, with limited success in age‐related liver diseases progression models [ 34 , 35 ] and to improve aged immune response [ 36 ]. Another factor that could affect the hemolytic activity of D + Q is the specific stimulus used to induce senescence. D + Q has primarily been tested in radiation‐induced senescence models, whereas our study used other senescence‐inducing stimuli. It is possible that the specific targets of the D + Q combination, and therefore its senolytic action, are not activated in our model. This suggests that the development and activation of SCAPs might depend on the senescence‐inducing stimulus, leading to differential effects of D + Q across models [ 37 ].

Studying SCAPs and their intricate interactions within cellular networks offers a promising avenue for advancing our understanding of cellular aging and the development of age‐related pathologies. Our findings underscore the complexity of the senescence‐associated antiapoptotic mechanisms and highlight the potential for beneficially targeting these pathways to modulate senescence. As we continue to unravel the multifaceted roles of SCAPs in cellular health and disease, integrating this knowledge into clinical strategies could lead to innovative treatments that delay the onset of age‐related diseases and enhance the quality of life in aging populations. Future research should focus on translating these molecular insights into practical applications, ensuring that the potential of senolytics to treat or prevent age‐related conditions is fully realized.
sections.conclusion:
In this work, we propose that the development and activation of SCAPs result from changes in co‐expression patterns that occur in response to the induction and progression of senescence. Therefore, the emergence of these transcriptional survival programs could be independent of the expression levels of their genes. This study proposes a novel computational approach to identify potential SCAPs and senolytic molecules, combining transcriptomic profiling analysis, gene co‐expression networks, and network pharmacology. Thus, targeting small molecules to the SCAPs GCNs could be a good pharmacological approach that allows the discovery and repositioning of new molecules with senolytic activity. This targeting strategy is supported by our findings of the multifunctional roles of these genes in cellular networks that influence metabolic, differentiation, and inflammatory pathways, underlining their potential broad impact on cell physiology.

One hundred and twenty SCAP candidate genes were identified, of which 18 are proposed as novel SCAP targets of known senolytics. Network pharmacology analysis revealed more than 600 molecules with potential senolytic activity, many with multitarget mechanisms.

We found that Fluorouracil acts as a senolytic through a multitarget mechanism involving the inhibition of AURKA, EGFR, IRS1, SMAD4, and KRAS. We consider these targets as new SCAPs since their transcriptomic signature profile is similar to that of the original SCAPs, their genes are co‐expressed with the genes of the original SCAPs, forming a dense network, and their pharmacological inhibition leads to a reduction in the functionality of senescent cells. This decrease in functionality is attributed to the induction of selective apoptosis. The interaction of these genes within cellular networks provides a new understanding of how SCAPs contribute to cell survival under stress conditions induced by aging and pathological states. However, considering the polypharmacological nature of fluorouracil, the senolytic effect could be given by inhibiting its other targets. Furthermore, the differential effects observed between the SIPS and RS models suggest that the context and type of senescence induction critically influence the effectiveness of senolytic interventions.

In the future studies, we aim to perform gene silencing experiments targeting AURKA, EGFR, IRS1, SMAD4, and KRAS using siRNA or shRNA across various cell types and responding to senescence stimuli. These experiments will deepen our understanding of their roles as SCAPs. Furthermore, we plan to employ advanced techniques such as single‐cell sequencing alongside functional and comparative genomics approaches to gain more comprehensive insights into the dynamics and complexity of how survival and antiapoptotic resistance networks develop. Through these approaches, we aim to elucidate the specific contributions of each SCAPs to the cellular resistance mechanisms and their potential as therapeutic targets. This work lays the foundation for future functional validation studies of the newly identified SCAPs and the development of more effective and specific senolytic interventions. By integrating these methods, we will enhance our understanding of the components and mechanisms underpinning senescence and resistance to apoptosis.
